    <div class="guide-header">
        <span class="guide-badge"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Identity & Access Management</span>
        <h1>OAuth Security in 2026: How Attackers Exploit the Protocol You Trust</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">From trusted authorization standard to attack vector
            — device code phishing, redirection abuse, consent phishing, token persistence, and how to defend your
            organization</p>
        <div style="margin-top: 1rem; color: var(--text-muted);">
            <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 20 min read</span> <span style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Intermediate to Advanced</span> <span
                style="margin: 0 0.5rem;">|</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> March 2026</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <img src="/images/guides/oauth-security-attacks-defense-2026.webp"
        alt="OAuth Security Attacks and Defense Guide 2026" class="featured-image"
        style="width: 100%; max-width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 12px; margin: 2rem 0; box-shadow: 0 10px 40px rgba(245,158,11,0.2); border: 1px solid var(--border);"
        loading="lazy">

    <div class="warning-box" style="margin-bottom: 2rem;">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-balance-scale"></i> Research Ethics & Responsible Disclosure:</strong>
        This guide is published for defensive security research and educational purposes. Attack techniques
        described are based on publicly disclosed research from Microsoft Threat Intelligence, CISA advisories, and
        peer-reviewed security publications. Organizations are encouraged to use this material to assess and improve
        their OAuth security posture.
    </div>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-file-alt"></i> Abstract:</strong>
        OAuth 2.0 has been the backbone of delegated authorization on the internet for over a decade. In 2025-2026,
        threat actors including Storm-2372 and operators of Phishing-as-a-Service platforms like Tycoon 2FA are
        exploiting legitimate OAuth features — device code flow, error-triggered redirections, and consent pages —
        to bypass MFA and gain persistent access to Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace accounts. This guide explains
        how OAuth works, why it was considered secure, what has changed, and provides verified defensive measures
        including Conditional Access policies, KQL detection queries, and app governance strategies.
    </div>

    <!-- SECTION 1 -->
    <h2 id="what-is-oauth">1. What Is OAuth 2.0 and Why Was It Trusted?</h2>

    <h3>1.1 The Problem OAuth Solved</h3>
    <p>Before OAuth, if a third-party application needed to access your data on another service (e.g., a calendar
        app reading your Gmail), you had to hand over your actual username and password. This was fundamentally
        broken — the third party had full access, couldn't be selectively revoked, and if compromised, exposed your
        entire account.</p>

    <p>OAuth 2.0, defined in <strong>RFC 6749</strong> (published October 2012), solved this by introducing
        <strong>delegated authorization</strong>. Instead of sharing passwords, users grant specific, scoped
        permissions to applications via tokens. The key principles were:</p>

    <ul>
        <li><strong>No password sharing</strong> — The third-party app never sees your password</li>
        <li><strong>Scoped access</strong> — Apps only get the permissions they request (e.g., "read email" but not
            "send email")</li>
        <li><strong>Revocable tokens</strong> — Users can revoke access without changing their password</li>
        <li><strong>Time-limited</strong> — Access tokens expire, requiring refresh</li>
    </ul>

    <h3>1.2 Why OAuth Was Considered Secure</h3>
    <p>For over a decade, OAuth 2.0 was widely regarded as a secure authorization framework because:</p>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Security Property</th>
                <th>How OAuth Achieves It</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Credential Isolation</strong></td>
                <td>User credentials are only entered on the Identity Provider's domain (e.g.,
                    <code>login.microsoftonline.com</code>), never on the third-party app</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Least Privilege</strong></td>
                <td>Scopes limit what an app can access — users see exactly what permissions are requested</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Token Expiration</strong></td>
                <td>Access tokens are short-lived (typically 1 hour for Microsoft Entra ID), limiting the window of
                    compromise</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Client Authentication</strong></td>
                <td>Confidential clients must authenticate with client secrets or certificates at the token endpoint
                </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Redirect URI Validation</strong></td>
                <td>Authorization servers validate redirect URIs against pre-registered values, preventing code
                    interception</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>PKCE (RFC 7636)</strong></td>
                <td>Proof Key for Code Exchange prevents authorization code interception in public clients</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-info-circle"></i> Key Insight:</strong>
        <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">The OAuth 2.0 specification itself is not broken. What
            attackers are exploiting in 2025-2026 are <strong>legitimate, by-design features</strong> of the
            protocol — the same redirect behavior, device code flow, and consent mechanisms that make OAuth flexible
            are being weaponized. This is what makes these attacks so difficult to detect — they use trusted
            infrastructure.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- SECTION 2 -->
    <h2 id="oauth-flows">2. How OAuth 2.0 Works: The Authorization Code Flow</h2>

    <p>The <strong>Authorization Code Flow</strong> is the most common and recommended OAuth 2.0 grant type for web
        applications. Understanding it is essential before examining how attackers subvert it.</p>

    <div class="architecture-diagram">
        <pre style="color: var(--accent-cyan); margin: 0;">

┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ USER │ │ CLIENT │ │ AUTH SERVER │ │ (Browser)│ │ (Your App) │ │ (Entra ID / │ │ │ │ │ │ Google) │ └────┬─────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ 1. Click “Login │ │ │ with Microsoft” │ │ │──────────────────────>│ │ │ │ 2. Redirect to │ │ │ /authorize endpoint │ │<──────────────────────│ with: │ │ │ - client_id │ │ │ - redirect_uri │ │ │ - scope │ │ │ - state (CSRF token) │ │ │ - code_challenge │ │ 3. User sees login │ (PKCE) │ │ page on TRUSTED │ │ │ domain (Microsoft) │ │ │──────────────────────────────────────────────>│ │ │ │ │ 4. User enters │ │ │ credentials + MFA │ │ │──────────────────────────────────────────────>│ │ │ │ │ 5. Auth server │ │ │ redirects back with │ │ │ authorization CODE │ │ │<──────────────────────────────────────────────│ │──────────────────────>│ │ │ │ 6. Exchange code │ │ │ for tokens (backchannel) │ │──────────────────────>│ │ │ │ │ │ 7. Access Token + │ │ │ Refresh Token │ │ │<──────────────────────│ │ 8. User is logged in │ │ │<──────────────────────│ │ 

    <h3>2.2 The Four OAuth 2.0 Grant Types</h3>
    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Grant Type</th>
                <th>Use Case</th>
                <th>Security Level</th>
                <th>2026 Risk</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Authorization Code + PKCE</strong></td>
                <td>Web apps, mobile apps, SPAs</td>
                <td class="severity-high">Most Secure</td>
                <td>Low — if properly implemented</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Client Credentials</strong></td>
                <td>Server-to-server (no user)</td>
                <td class="severity-high">Secure</td>
                <td>Medium — over-privileged app registrations</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Device Code</strong></td>
                <td>Smart TVs, IoT, CLI tools</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">⚠️ HIGH RISK</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Critical — Storm-2372 phishing vector</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Implicit (Deprecated)</strong></td>
                <td>Legacy SPAs</td>
                <td class="severity-critical">Insecure</td>
                <td>Should be completely disabled</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <!-- SECTION 3 -->
    <h2 id="what-changed">3. What Changed: The 2025-2026 Attack Landscape</h2>

    <p>So if OAuth itself isn't broken, what changed? Three converging trends created the current threat landscape:
    </p>

    <h3>3.1 Identity Became the Perimeter</h3>
    <p>As organizations adopted cloud-first architectures, the traditional network perimeter dissolved. Identity —
        specifically, OAuth tokens — became the primary access mechanism. Microsoft reported in its 2025 Digital
        Defense Report that <strong>identity-based attacks are now the #1 initial access vector</strong>, surpassing
        traditional network exploits.</p>

    <h3>3.2 Phishing-as-a-Service Industrialized MFA Bypass</h3>
    <p>Platforms like <strong>Tycoon 2FA</strong> democratized Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks. By mid-2025,
        Microsoft reported that Tycoon 2FA was responsible for approximately <strong>62% of all phishing attempts
            blocked</strong> by their systems. The platform was eventually dismantled by Europol in a coordinated
        takedown of 330 domains, but the techniques it popularized persist.</p>

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-chart-bar"></i> By The Numbers (Microsoft Telemetry, 2025):</strong>
        <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem;">
            <li><strong>146% increase</strong> in AiTM phishing incidents year-over-year</li>
            <li><strong>~40,000 AiTM incidents</strong> detected daily</li>
            <li><strong>62%</strong> of phishing blocked was Tycoon 2FA (before takedown)</li>
            <li><strong>96,000+ distinct victims</strong> linked to Tycoon 2FA globally</li>
            <li><strong>13 million malicious emails</strong> blocked in October 2025 alone</li>
        </ul>
    </div>

    <h3>3.3 Nation-State Actors Adopted OAuth Abuse</h3>
    <p>In February 2025, Microsoft Threat Intelligence published an advisory on <strong>Storm-2372</strong>, a
        threat actor assessed with moderate confidence to align with Russian interests. Storm-2372 pioneered a new
        phishing technique that abuses the OAuth Device Authorization Grant flow — a legitimate protocol feature —
        to bypass MFA entirely. This marked a shift from exploiting vulnerabilities to exploiting <em>features</em>.
    </p>

    <!-- SECTION 4 -->
    <h2 id="device-code">4. Attack Vector 1: Device Code Phishing (Storm-2372)</h2>

    <p>The Device Authorization Grant (defined in <strong>RFC 8628</strong>) was designed for devices with limited
        input capabilities — smart TVs, IoT devices, and CLI tools. The user authenticates on a separate device
        (like their phone) by entering a short code displayed on the limited device.</p>

    <div class="attack-scenario">
        <p><strong>How Storm-2372 Weaponized It:</strong></p>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Social Engineering:</strong> Attackers establish rapport with targets via WhatsApp, Signal,
                or Microsoft Teams, often impersonating prominent individuals relevant to the target's organization
            </li>
            <li><strong>Fake Meeting Invite:</strong> The attacker sends a phishing email disguised as a Microsoft
                Teams meeting invitation</li>
            <li><strong>Device Code Delivery:</strong> The invitation contains an attacker-generated device code and
                directs the victim to <code>https://microsoft.com/devicelogin</code> — a completely
                <strong>legitimate Microsoft page</strong></li>
            <li><strong>Token Capture:</strong> When the victim enters the code and authenticates (including MFA),
                Microsoft issues OAuth tokens to the attacker's application, not the victim's</li>
            <li><strong>Persistent Access:</strong> The attacker captures both the access token and refresh token,
                gaining persistent access to the victim's Microsoft 365 account</li>
        </ol>
    </div>

    <div class="architecture-diagram">
        <pre style="color: var(--accent-cyan); margin: 0;">

STORM-2372 DEVICE CODE PHISHING ATTACK FLOW ════════════════════════════════════════════

┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ ATTACKER │ │ VICTIM │ │ MICROSOFT │ │ │ │ │ │ ENTRA ID │ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ │ │ │ 1. Request device code │ │───────────────────────────────────>│ │ │ │ 2. Receive: code=“GXLR93VF” │ │ (valid for 15 minutes) │ │<──────────────────────────────────│ │ │ │ │ 3. Send fake │ │ │ Teams invite │ │ │ with code │ │ │──────────────>│ │ │ │ │ │ │ 4. Victim goes to │ │ │ microsoft.com/ │ │ │ devicelogin │ │ │ (REAL Microsoft) │ │ │──────────────────>│ │ │ │ │ │ 5. Enters code │ │ │ + authenticates │ │ │ (including MFA!) │ │ │──────────────────>│ │ │ │ │ 6. Attacker polls token endpoint │ │───────────────────────────────────>│ │ │ │ 7. Receives access_token + │ │ refresh_token for victim │ │<──────────────────────────────────│ │ │ │ │ 8. Access victim’s M365 │ │ email, OneDrive, Teams… │ │ │ │ ▼ POST-EXPLOITATION: │ • Search inbox for “password”, │ “credentials”, “admin” │ • Exfiltrate sensitive emails │ • Send phishing from victim account │ • Register attacker device in │ Entra ID using PRT │ 

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Why This Is Devastating:</strong>
        <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">The victim authenticates on a <strong>real Microsoft
                page</strong>. There is no fake login form, no suspicious domain, no browser warning. The MFA
            challenge is satisfied legitimately. Traditional phishing defenses (URL reputation, browser warnings,
            email link scanning) are completely bypassed because every component of the flow uses legitimate
            Microsoft infrastructure.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>4.1 Evolved Tactic: Primary Refresh Token (PRT) Abuse</h3>
    <p>In February 2025, Microsoft observed Storm-2372 evolving their technique. After capturing tokens via device
        code phishing, the attackers began using the <strong>Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID</strong> to:
    </p>
    <ol>
        <li>Obtain a refresh token with broker capabilities</li>
        <li>Register an attacker-controlled device in Entra ID</li>
        <li>Acquire a <strong>Primary Refresh Token (PRT)</strong></li>
        <li>Use the PRT to access organizational resources as a "trusted device"</li>
    </ol>
    <p>This technique grants the attacker persistent, device-level trust within the organization — significantly
        more dangerous than simple token theft.</p>

    <!-- SECTION 5 -->
    <h2 id="redirection">5. Attack Vector 2: OAuth Redirection Abuse</h2>

    <p>This technique, disclosed by multiple security researchers in 2025 and confirmed by Microsoft, exploits a
        fundamental aspect of OAuth's design: <strong>error-triggered redirections</strong>.</p>

    <div class="attack-scenario">
        <p><strong>How It Works:</strong></p>
        <ol>
            <li>Attackers register a malicious application in an attacker-controlled Entra ID tenant</li>
            <li>They configure the app's redirect URI to point to an attacker-owned domain</li>
            <li>They craft a phishing URL targeting
                <code>login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/authorize</code> with intentionally malformed
                parameters (e.g., invalid scopes or <code>prompt=none</code>)</li>
            <li>When the authorization server processes the request and encounters an error, it performs a
                standards-compliant redirect to the registered redirect URI — which is the attacker's domain</li>
            <li>The victim is now on the attacker's site, which may serve credential-harvesting pages or malware
                downloads</li>
        </ol>
    </div>

    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Example Malicious OAuth URL (for awareness — DO NOT use)</h3>
        <pre><code># This URL originates from a TRUSTED Microsoft domain

Email filters and browsers will NOT flag it

https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/authorize ?client_id=ATTACKER_APP_ID &response_type=code &redirect_uri=hxxps://attacker-site.com/callback &scope=INVALID_SCOPE_TO_TRIGGER_ERROR &prompt=none

Result: Microsoft’s auth server redirects to:

hxxps://attacker-site.com/callback?error=invalid_scope

→ User is now on the attacker’s phishing site

→ The URL they clicked was login.microsoftonline.com

→ All email/browser reputation checks passed

    </div>

    <p><strong>Why traditional defenses fail:</strong> The phishing link originates from
        <code>login.microsoftonline.com</code> or <code>accounts.google.com</code> — domains with perfect reputation
        scores. Email gateway filters, URL scanners, and browser Safe Browsing all trust these domains implicitly.
        Microsoft has confirmed these campaigns target government and public-sector organizations.</p>

    <!-- SECTION 6 -->
    <h2 id="consent">6. Attack Vector 3: Consent Phishing & Illicit App Grants</h2>

    <p>Consent phishing takes advantage of OAuth's consent mechanism — the permission dialog users see when granting
        an application access to their data.</p>

    <h3>6.1 The Attack</h3>
    <p>Attackers register an OAuth application that appears legitimate — often impersonating known brands or using
        names similar to popular internal tools. They then trick users (via phishing or social engineering) into
        granting this application broad OAuth permissions. Once consent is granted, the application receives OAuth
        tokens that provide ongoing access to the user's data.</p>

    <table>
        <thead>
            <tr>
                <th>Aspect</th>
                <th>Legitimate App</th>
                <th>Malicious App</th>
            </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Publisher</strong></td>
                <td>Verified publisher badge</td>
                <td>Unverified or spoofed publisher</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Permissions</strong></td>
                <td>Minimal scopes (e.g., <code>User.Read</code>)</td>
                <td>Broad scopes (e.g., <code>Mail.ReadWrite</code>, <code>Files.ReadWrite.All</code>)</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>Access Duration</strong></td>
                <td>Short-lived, scoped to session</td>
                <td>Persistent via refresh tokens</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td><strong>MFA Required</strong></td>
                <td>Yes, at authentication</td>
                <td>Bypassed — consent is post-authentication</td>
            </tr>
        </tbody>
    </table>

    <div class="warning-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Critical Risk:</strong>
        <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Once a user grants consent, the malicious app has
            persistent access. <strong>Changing the user's password does not revoke the OAuth grant.</strong> The
            attacker maintains access until the admin explicitly revokes the application's consent in Entra ID or
            Google Workspace admin console.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- SECTION 7 -->
    <h2 id="token-persistence">7. Attack Vector 4: Token Persistence & Theft</h2>

    <p>OAuth tokens, by design, provide access without requiring re-authentication. This property — essential for
        user experience — creates significant security implications when tokens are stolen.</p>

    <h3>7.1 Why Token Theft Persists After Password Reset</h3>
    <p>A common misconception is that resetting a user's password invalidates all active sessions. With OAuth, this
        is <strong>not automatically true</strong>:</p>

    <ul>
        <li><strong>Access tokens</strong> remain valid until they expire (typically 60-90 minutes for Entra ID)
        </li>
        <li><strong>Refresh tokens</strong> can have lifetimes of days to months depending on configuration</li>
        <li>Password reset does NOT automatically revoke existing refresh tokens in all configurations</li>
        <li>Attackers who obtain a refresh token can silently generate new access tokens without any user
            interaction</li>
    </ul>

    <h3>7.2 Token Theft via Infostealer Malware</h3>
    <p>Modern infostealer malware (RedLine, Raccoon, Vidar) specifically targets OAuth and session tokens stored in
        browser profiles. These tokens are extracted alongside cookies and sent to attacker C2 servers, enabling
        session hijacking without triggering MFA.</p>

    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Where Tokens Are Stored (Browser Forensics Reference)</h3>
        <pre><code># Chrome/Edge token storage locations (for forensic analysis only)

Windows:

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Local Storage
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Cookies

macOS:

~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Cookies ~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft Edge/Default/Cookies

Infostealers target these files to extract:

- Session cookies (bypass MFA entirely)

- OAuth refresh tokens (persistent access)

- Saved passwords (credential stuffing)

    </div>

    <h3>7.3 Shadow Google Accounts</h3>
    <p>A vulnerability identified by security researchers affects Google OAuth specifically. When employees use
        "Sign in with Google" for third-party services (Slack, Zoom, Notion), they may create OAuth grants that
        persist even after the employee is offboarded. If the organization doesn't revoke these OAuth connections,
        former employees retain access to corporate resources through these "shadow" OAuth sessions. Google has
        begun automatically deleting unused OAuth clients to address this.</p>

    <!-- SECTION 8 -->
    <h2 id="defense">8. Defense: Conditional Access, App Governance & Detection</h2>

    <h3>8.1 Block Device Code Flow (Critical)</h3>
    <p>The single most impactful mitigation against Storm-2372 and similar attacks is to <strong>block the device
            code authentication flow</strong> via Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra ID.</p>

    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Entra ID — Block Device Code Flow via Conditional Access</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-json">// Conditional Access Policy — Block Device Code Flow

// Source: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Advisory (Feb 2025) { “displayName”: “Block Device Code Authentication Flow”, “state”: “enabled”, “conditions”: { “users”: { “includeUsers”: [“All”] }, “applications”: { “includeApplications”: [“All”] }, “authenticationFlows”: { “transferMethods”: [“deviceCodeFlow”] } }, “grantControls”: { “operator”: “OR”, “builtInControls”: [“block”] } } 

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Implementation Note:</strong>
        <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Before blocking device code flow globally, audit your
            organization for legitimate uses. Common legitimate uses include: conference room displays, Azure CLI on
            shared terminals, and IoT devices. For these, create an exception policy that allows device code flow
            only from specific trusted network locations or compliant devices.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>8.2 Restrict OAuth App Registrations</h3>
    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> PowerShell — Restrict User Consent to Verified Publishers Only</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-powershell"># Restrict user consent to apps from verified publishers only

Requires: Microsoft.Graph PowerShell module

Source: Microsoft Entra ID documentation

Connect-MgGraph -Scopes “Policy.ReadWrite.Authorization”

Set consent policy: users can only consent to apps

from verified publishers, and only for low-risk permissions

Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -DefaultUserRolePermissions @{ PermissionGrantPoliciesAssigned = @( “managePermissionGrantsForSelf.microsoft-user-default-low” ) }

Verify the change

Get-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy | Select-Object -ExpandProperty DefaultUserRolePermissions | Select-Object PermissionGrantPoliciesAssigned

Expected output: microsoft-user-default-low

This means users can only consent to:

- Apps from verified publishers

- For permissions classified as “low impact”

All other consent requests require admin approval

    </div>

    <h3>8.3 Revoke Compromised Tokens</h3>
    <p>If device code phishing or token theft is suspected, immediately revoke all refresh tokens for the affected
        user:</p>
    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Emergency Token Revocation (Microsoft Graph API)</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-bash"># Revoke all refresh tokens for a compromised user

Source: Microsoft Graph API documentation

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/user-revokesigninsessions

Using Microsoft Graph API

POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/{userId}/revokeSignInSessions

Using Azure CLI

az rest –method POST
–url “https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/compromised@company.com/revokeSignInSessions”

Using PowerShell

Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId “compromised@company.com”

IMPORTANT: After revocation, also:

1. Reset the user’s password

2. Require MFA re-registration

3. Review and revoke any suspicious OAuth app consents

4. Check for attacker-registered devices in Entra ID

    </div>

    <h3>8.4 Audit OAuth App Permissions Regularly</h3>
    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> PowerShell — Audit High-Privilege OAuth Apps in Entra ID</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-powershell"># List all OAuth apps with high-privilege permissions

Source: Microsoft Graph PowerShell documentation

Connect-MgGraph -Scopes “Application.Read.All”,“DelegatedPermissionGrant.Read.All”

Find all delegated permission grants (user consents)

$grants = Get-MgOauth2PermissionGrant -All

Filter for high-risk scopes

$highRiskScopes = @(“Mail.ReadWrite”, “Mail.Send”, “Files.ReadWrite.All”, “Directory.ReadWrite.All”, “User.ReadWrite.All”)

$riskyGrants = $grants | Where-Object { $highRiskScopes | ForEach-Object { $grant.Scope -match $_ } }

Output for review

$riskyGrants | ForEach-Object { $app = Get-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $.ClientId [PSCustomObject]@{ AppName = $app.DisplayName Scopes = $.Scope ConsentType = $.ConsentType UserId = $.PrincipalId } } | Format-Table -AutoSize 

    <!-- SECTION 9 -->
    <h2 id="detection">9. Detection Engineering: KQL & Sigma Rules</h2>

    <h3>9.1 KQL — Detect Device Code Phishing Attempts</h3>
    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Microsoft Sentinel KQL — Device Code Phishing Detection</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-sql">// Detect suspicious device code authentication patterns

// Source: Adapted from Microsoft Storm-2372 advisory // Deploy in: Microsoft Sentinel Analytics Rules

SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where AuthenticationProtocol == “deviceCode” | where ResultType == 0 // Successful sign-ins only | extend DeviceDetail = parse_json(DeviceDetail) | extend LocationDetail = parse_json(LocationDetails) | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location = strcat(LocationDetail.city, “, “, LocationDetail.countryOrRegion), DeviceOS = DeviceDetail.operatingSystem, IsManaged = DeviceDetail.isManaged, ConditionalAccessStatus | where IsManaged != true // Unmanaged devices are suspicious | summarize AttemptCount = count(), DistinctIPs = dcount(IPAddress), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName), Locations = make_set(Location) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where AttemptCount > 1 or DistinctIPs > 1 

    <h3>9.2 Sigma Rule — OAuth Consent Phishing Detection</h3>
    <div class="technical-box">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-terminal"></i> Sigma Rule: Suspicious OAuth Application Consent</h3>
        <pre><code class="language-yaml">title: Suspicious OAuth Application Consent Grant

id: a2c1b3d4-oauth-consent-2026 status: experimental description: | Detects when a user grants consent to an OAuth application with high-privilege permissions from an unverified publisher, which may indicate consent phishing. author: TheHGTech Security Research date: 2026/03/06 references: - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/ - https://thehgtech.com/guides/oauth-security-attacks-defense-2026.html logsource: product: azure service: auditlogs detection: selection: Category: “ApplicationManagement” ActivityDisplayName: “Consent to application” filter_verified: TargetResources.modifiedProperties.newValue|contains: - “IsVerifiedPublisher: true” condition: selection and not filter_verified falsepositives: - Internal line-of-business applications - Development/test applications level: high tags: - attack.initial_access - attack.t1566 - attack.t1550.001 

    <!-- SECTION 10 -->
    <h2 id="checklist">10. OAuth Security Hardening Checklist</h2>

    <div class="success-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-clipboard-check"></i> Priority Actions for Security Teams:</strong>
        <table style="margin-top: 1rem;">
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Priority</th>
                    <th>Action</th>
                    <th>Mitigates</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-critical">P0</td>
                    <td>Block device code flow via Conditional Access</td>
                    <td>Storm-2372, device code phishing</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-critical">P0</td>
                    <td>Restrict user consent to verified publishers only</td>
                    <td>Consent phishing, illicit app grants</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-critical">P0</td>
                    <td>Deploy phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)</td>
                    <td>AiTM, token interception</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-high">P1</td>
                    <td>Audit all existing OAuth app permissions quarterly</td>
                    <td>Over-privileged apps, shadow access</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-high">P1</td>
                    <td>Configure token lifetime policies (reduce refresh token lifetime)</td>
                    <td>Token persistence attacks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td class="severity-high">P1</td>
                    <td>Enable Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)</td>
                    <td>Stolen token reuse</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>P2</td>
                    <td>Deploy KQL/Sigma detection rules from this guide</td>
                    <td>Device code phishing, consent abuse</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>P2</td>
                    <td>Implement app governance policies in Defender for Cloud Apps</td>
                    <td>Unauthorized app access</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>P2</td>
                    <td>Revoke OAuth grants for offboarded employees</td>
                    <td>Shadow accounts, persistent access</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>P2</td>
                    <td>Train users to recognize device code and consent phishing</td>
                    <td>Social engineering</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>
    </div>
